request: Do the heavy versus light ball drop as a prediction moment for my physics students.
intent: Physics students should commit to a prediction before seeing the answer.
goal: The viewer predicts, sees both balls land together, and knows why.
promise: Two very different balls, one question, and a guess before the answer.
arc: Two balls held at the top, a long pause to guess, the drop side by side, the reason.

events.text: A bowling ball and a tennis ball, dropped from the same height, at the same moment.
events.look: the two balls side by side at the same height

withhold.what: the balls falling and which lands first

events.look: the two balls held at the top

holds.does: both balls hang at the top; nothing moves toward the answer

events.text: They land together. Gravity speeds up every object at the same rate, whatever its mass.
events.knows: They land together; gravity accelerates every mass equally.
events.look: the two balls falling level with each other

demo.what: both balls falling side by side

phases.why: a fall slow enough to see they stay level the whole way

events.text: Only air resistance can split them. And for these two, it barely matters.
events.knows: Air resistance is the only thing that can separate them.

quiz.a: Gravity speeds up every object at the same rate, whatever its mass.

quiz.q: What can make them land at different times?
Where were the balls during the pause before the answer?
quiz.a: Held at the top, side by side, not yet falling.
